languagePolicy.ordinaryVocabularyRule: Use fully established ordinary Turkish vocabulary regardless of historical etymology. Do not replace a natural Turkish word merely because it entered Turkish from another language.
languagePolicy.religiousLabelRule: Do not use a conventional religious technical label as a substitute for translating the source occurrence. Express the occurrence-specific act or concept in transparent Turkish whenever the label would conceal its source-grounded meaning.
languagePolicy.properNameRule: Retain Allah as the source proper name.
languagePolicy.fallbackRule: When no single natural word is adequate, write a short, transparent Turkish phrase.

grammarSupport.guidance: Target languages should preserve the direct command force and its second-person addressee rather than recast it as a statement.
If the target language requires an explicit possessor or addressee, it should keep the suffix as the discourse addressee rather than inventing a lexical antecedent.
Target languages with obligatory objects may be tempted to supply what was created, but the Arabic leaves the object of خَلَقَ unexpressed.
Target languages may be forced to saturate the object of سَوَّىٰ, but the Arabic keeps the object compressed.
A single-ayah rendering may detach the relative clause from the divine noun phrase it continues or add an explanatory noun not present in the Arabic.
Target languages with obligatory objects may supply what was determined, but قَدَّرَ has no expressed object in the Arabic.
Target languages may require an object for هَدَىٰ, but the Arabic leaves the guided entity or domain unexpressed.
Rendering this ayah alone may obscure that both verbs share the same relative-chain antecedent rather than introducing a new subject.
The relative opening and following transformation in 87:5 need the local chain so a target-language reader does not treat the subject or object as newly introduced.
Target languages that require an explicit object noun should resolve the suffix to the nearby pasture object without turning the result complement into its antecedent.
Word-for-word rendering may misread غُثَاءً as a separate object rather than the result state of the made object.
Target languages may ask what will not be forgotten, but the Arabic does not express an object for تَنسَىٰ.
The negation should remain scoped over تَنسَىٰ as the result of the promise, not be flattened into an unrelated prohibition or wish.
If the target language requires an explicit subject for the future verb, it should track the first common plural speaker role rather than a local noun antecedent.

grammarSupport.guidance: The exception phrase must remain attached to the preceding negated forgetting claim, not read as an independent condition.
Starting at إِلَّا without 87:6 can hide the negated clause whose scope the exception restricts.
The emphatic إِنَّ clause should not be reduced to a bare new sentence that loses the resumptive reference to ٱللَّهُ.
If an explicit subject is required for يَعْلَمُ, it should resume ٱللَّهُ rather than a vague prior proposition.
Target languages may need a goal or suitability complement rather than treating لِلْيُسْرَىٰ as a simple direct object.
The repeated second-person object and first-plural speaker chain may be obscured if this promise is rendered apart from the surrounding address.
Target languages with obligatory objects may supply who or what is reminded, but ذَكِّرْ has no expressed object in the Arabic.
The command force and its second-person addressee should be preserved rather than treated as a neutral statement about reminding.
The conditional phrase should scope over the command as its protasis, not be rendered as a detached temporal or causal clause.
The following ayah identifies the class for whom the reminder takes effect, so an isolated rendering can over-specify the condition.
Target languages may ask what مَن يَخْشَىٰ fears, but the Arabic leaves the object of يَخْشَىٰ unexpressed.
The headless relative مَن يَخْشَىٰ should remain the subject of سَيَذَّكَّرُ rather than becoming an independent clause.
This response line should be read with the preceding command and condition so the beneficiary of reminder is not over-identified beyond the Arabic.
The feminine object suffix may be rendered as a vague object unless the reminder contrast in 87:9-11 is kept visible.
The relative clause may sound headless in translation unless its masculine antecedent in 87:11 remains available.

ayat.arabicText: ثُمَّ لَا يَمُوتُ فِيهَا وَلَا يَحْيَىٰ

grammarSupport.guidance: The locative suffix and carried subject can be misassigned if 87:13 is translated without the fire and its sufferer from 87:12.
The paired negation must stay over both predicates rather than collapsing into a single simple verb phrase.
The certifying particle may need explicit perfective or emphatic force in target languages that otherwise make the success claim sound merely general.
The subject of the coordinated perfect verbs and the possessor in رَبِّهِۦ may be expanded as a new actor unless the headless relative in 87:14 remains active.
Target languages with overt subjects may need a plural addressee while the Arabic gives only second-person plural agreement.
The comparison may require an explicit standard such as what worldly life is preferred over, but Arabic leaves that standard unexpressed until the contrast with 87:17.
Rendering بَلْ as simple addition can lose the corrective turn from the prior successful devotee to the addressed group.
Single-ayah rendering may supply the wrong comparison standard for تُؤْثِرُونَ.
The comparative predicate may require an explicit standard in translation, while Arabic compresses the standard recoverable from 87:16.
The second comparative predicate may require the same supplied standard, but Arabic leaves it shared with the prior comparison.
The paired comparatives can be underspecified or over-specified unless the preceding worldly-life object supplies their comparison standard.
An explicit target-language antecedent for هَٰذَا would choose between the broader admonition and the nearest afterlife comparison.
The stacked إِنَّ plus لَ emphasis may need force in translation without duplicating the assertion awkwardly.
Reading only 87:18 can make هَٰذَا look like a fixed local noun phrase rather than a demonstrative over prior discourse.
As a standalone ayah, صُحُفِ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ وَمُوسَىٰ may be translated as an independent fragment rather than apposition to the former scriptures in 87:18.
The two proper names should be kept as coordinated possessors of صُحُف rather than as separate scripture titles.
